Steps the shaft animation counters: $1C counts 0-5 (at 6 it wraps and moves the map marker's Y $28 by one), $1B counts 0-2.

Puts the flashing marker on the pocket computer's map: sprite 6 at ($27, $28), its colour cycling every four ticks through tbl_marker_colours; then reads the map cell under it ($B761) and writes that character into the map on screen ($428A + rows).
Eight colours the map marker cycles through: black, dark grey, grey, light grey, white, light grey, grey, dark grey.
Paints the six piece slots of the display in their pieces' colours ($98-$9D through $7A37) and colours the column between the halves (column $0D of rows $DA8D-$DB55) yellow (7).

Scrolls the shaft view up by one row as the lift descends: rows $4028 onwards copied to the row above, screen and colour RAM, columns 0-16 and then 23-39 (two passes, $E4). First clears the corridor marker ($1D) by restoring $4011-$4016 from $0D00.
Scrolls the shaft view down by one row as the lift rises: 14 rows of 40 characters from $4208 upwards, unrolled. First restores $4241-$4246 if $1E is set.

Colours the two corridor openings (left and right, X = 1 and 0) from their state $1F/$20: different colours (8, 1, the corridor's own $23/$24, 9) by how far the opening has scrolled into view, through the row address tables $0E50/$0E5E.
Operand low byte of `sta $D800,y` in colour_corridors: the colour row's address, from the row table $0E50.
High byte of the colour row address in colour_corridors, from $0E5E.
Writes colour A into 17 cells of one row of colour RAM, row Y from $0E50/$0E5E (self-modified operand), ending at the column $0DD4,x.
Operand low byte of `sta $D800,y` in colour_row16, from $0E50.
High byte of the row address in colour_row16, from $0E5E.

Draws the row that scrolls in at the top while the lift rises, for both sides: rock, the corridor's floor ($0E28), ceiling ($0DD8), wall ($0E00) or opening, from each side's state $1F/$20 and the map ($7875). A side reaching state $15 starts a new corridor.
Draws the row that scrolls in at the bottom while the lift descends; the mirror of shaft_new_row_top, using the map at $786D.
Entry of shaft_new_row_bottom's end: draws the corridor opening at the bottom of the shaft view if the map has one there ($786D), used when the agent comes out of a room ($AFA5).
Draws the eight characters of the corridor marker at $4010 from $0DC0 in colour $0F and sets $1D: the corridor below is in view.
Map cell for the row below the lift: Y offset $28 - $BB, then map_cell.
Map cell for the row above the lift: Y offset $28 - $B8, then map_cell.
Reads the stronghold map cell at map row A/8 and column $27 - $6B + (A AND 7), from the row table at $78A4; returns $FF if the row is above the map. Y is preserved.
Six row addresses of the map that the shaft view reads: $FC08, $FC90, $FD18, $FDA0, $FE28, $FEB0.
High bytes of the addresses in tbl_map_rows.
Index of the map square under the marker: row ($28 - $B8)/8 times 9 plus column ($27 - $6B)/16, in Y, for the tables at $FF96. Entering at $78B5 takes the row offset in A.
Entry of map_room_index with the row offset already in A.

Colour of the room whose corridor appears below: map square from $28 - $BA (and one to the right when X is 0), the room number from $FF96, then the first byte of that room's record through the pointer table $0E70 (self-modified `lda` at $78FD). Y is preserved.
The same for the corridor appearing above ($28 - $B6).
Operand of `lda $1892` in corridor_colour: the room record's first byte (its colour), from the pointer table $0E70.
High byte of the room record address read by corridor_colour.

Flips the selected piece (slot $8F) top to bottom, animated: swaps the piece's rows with the display's work glyphs at $5C50 in ten steps two ticks apart ($7934 does one step, through self-modified operands at $7939/$793F). With no slot selected prints NO IMAGE SELECTED ($824A).

One step of flip_piece_v: exchanges six bytes, eight apart, between $5C50,x and the piece's data (Y counting down), then moves both indices to the next column, wrapping X at $30 to $58 and Y at $87 to $5F.
Operand low byte of `lda $5C50,x` in flip_v_step: the base of the glyphs being flipped (the display, or $5000 when build_piece flips a new piece).
High byte of the glyph base read by flip_v_step.
Operand low byte of `sta $5C50,x` in flip_v_step, set with $7939.
High byte of the glyph base written by flip_v_step.
Flips the selected piece left to right, animated in 21 steps one tick apart ($7999): each byte goes through the bit-reversal table at $C500. With no slot selected prints NO IMAGE SELECTED.
One step of flip_piece_h: exchanges three bytes between $5C50,x and the piece, reversing the bits of each through $C500, and steps the indices with wraps at $08 and $38.
Operand low byte of `lda $5C50,x` in flip_h_step: the base of the glyphs being mirrored.
High byte of the glyph base read by flip_h_step.
Operand low byte of `sta $5C50,x` in flip_h_step.
High byte of the glyph base written by flip_h_step.

Clears the selected slot of the display: saves the piece for undo ($7A89), zeroes its 144 bytes, marks the slot empty ($92,y), then selects the next occupied slot (skipping slot 3) or none ($8F = $FF, frame sprite 6 off). With no slot selected prints NO IMAGE SELECTED.

Gives the selected piece colour A (5, 7 or 3 from the colour keys): stores it in $98,y and paints the slot's 6 × 3 cells of colour RAM from tbl_slot_colour_ram. With no slot selected prints NO IMAGE SELECTED. Entered at $7A37 to paint slot Y without the check.
Entry of recolour_piece that paints slot Y in colour A without checking for a selection: used by paint_slots and remove_piece.
Low bytes of the colour RAM address of each display slot's top-left cell ($DA87, $DA8F, $DA96, $DAFF, $DB07, $DB0E with tbl_slot_colour_ram_hi).
High bytes for tbl_slot_colour_ram_lo: $DA, $DA, $DA, $DA, $DB, $DB.
The undo button: puts the piece saved at $C100 back into the slot it came from ($91), marks the slot used and selects it. With nothing saved ($91 negative) prints CAN'T UNDO ($8276).
Copies the 144 bytes of the selected slot's piece to the undo buffer at $C100 and remembers the slot in $91.

The top left key: scrolls the memory window one piece forward ($C3 + 1), animated over three steps: the glyphs at $5C50-$5E8F and their colour RAM ($DA87-$DB4F) shift up one place and the new piece ($4EF5 + $C3 + 2, colour $4F27) is drawn in ($9C47) at the bottom. Refuses with END OF MEMORY ($8260) when the next three entries are all empty (bit 7 set).
The middle left key: scrolls the memory window one piece back ($C3 - 1), the mirror of memory_forward. Refuses with END OF MEMORY at the start ($C3 = 0).

The bottom left key, the phone: sets $9F to show the hand is on the phone, clears the message window, hides sprites 5 and 6, saves the colour RAM of the window to $C220 and draws the phone's menu ($7C44, 8 rows of 22) with colours from $7C3C, the first two columns light blue (9). Limits the hand to the menu and parks it at its bottom.
Colours of the phone menu's eight rows, read last entry first: the first option cyan (3), the second purple (4), the blank row white (1), HANG UP yellow (7).

The phone's menu, 8 rows of 22 characters in the $5800 alphabet, with icon glyphs $22-$29 at the left: "CORRECT ORIENTATIONS / OF LEFTMOST PIECES", "HAVE WE ENOUGH / PIECES TO SOLVE THE / UPPER LEFT PUZZLE", "HANG UP".
The phone's four answers, 22 characters each in the $5800 alphabet: "A SOLUTION EXISTS", "NEED MORE PIECES", "ORIENTATION CORRECTED", "NOTHING IN MEMORY".

Prepares the SID for the phone: envelopes of voices 2 and 3 (attack/decay 0, sustain $F), their frequencies, a filter (cutoff $40, resonance off) and volume with filter mode $12, both voices gated with triangle ($11), and $A4 = 2 so the IRQ gates them off two frames later.

Fire on the phone's menu, by the hand's Y: below $C2 the first option (correct orientations, $7D9D), $C8-$E0 the second (enough pieces?, $7DE6), $E8 and below HANG UP ($7E05); the gaps between do nothing.

The first phone option: charges two minutes to the game clock ($83CC in decimal mode, interrupts off), points the dial table at $7E36 and the answer at $7F8D (self-modified `lda` at $7DCD and `jsr` at $7DE2), then dials: seven digits, each a dual tone ($7E44) a few ticks long with a gap; then the line ($7E9E) and the answer.
Operand low byte of `lda $7E36,x` in the phone's dialling loop: which number to dial ($7E36 or $7E3D).
High byte of the dial table address.
Operand low byte of the `jsr $7F8D` at the end of the dialling loop: the answer routine ($7F8D or $7FD7).
High byte of the answer routine's address.
The second phone option: as phone_ask_orient, with the dial table at $7E3D and the answer at $7FD7.
HANG UP: clears the message window, restores its colours from the copy at $C220, and returns the panel to the piece display (hand, memory, frames), volume back to 5.
The two numbers the phone dials, seven key indices each, read last first: 7, 6, 7, 8, 9, 0, 0 for the first option and 5, 5, 5, 4, 2, 1, 3 for the second. Index 0 is replaced by 11 (key 0).

Sounds key Y of the phone's keypad: voice 2 at the low tone and voice 3 at the high tone from tbl_dtmf (lo/hi bytes in four columns of twelve), volume 5 with the filter, both gated, gated off by the IRQ eight frames later.
The `rts` that ends dial_tone; the tone table read with `lda $7E6D,y` starts one byte later, at $7E6E, because the keys are numbered from 1.

The keypad's two-tone frequencies for dial_tone, four columns of twelve entries: voice 2 low and high bytes ($7E6E, $7E7A), voice 3 low and high bytes ($7E86, $7E92). Three keys share each row tone and each column tone, as on a touch-tone keypad.
Second column of tbl_dtmf: voice 2's high bytes.
Third column of tbl_dtmf: voice 3's low bytes.
Fourth column of tbl_dtmf: voice 3's high bytes.

The line after dialling: a random pause, a few random clicks ($7F54), another pause, twenty ring bursts on voices 2 and 3 (frequency $2880/$1E80), a random pause, more clicks, then the answer's sound: voices 2 and 3 with pulse waves, gated on and off over 80 ticks. Then returns to the answer routine.
One click on the phone line: voice 3 gated with triangle for a moment at volume 5.
Waits one tick: wait_ticks with A = 1.

Waits A ticks of the IRQ's counter $E0: adds A to $E0 and loops until $E0 equals the sum. Each pass calls `jsr $DD03`, which executes CIA 2's data direction register B: the start-up set it to $60, the opcode of `rts`, so the call returns at once. A copy whose start-up did not set it would crash here. Live (1 October 2026): $DD03 reads $60 in play and was executed 47,272 times in 120 frames; with $EA written there the program crashed.

Waits until the raster is past line $AB and then until it wraps to the top of the next frame (line below $AB again after the high lines), with interrupts off while it watches; used before turning the screen on or off.

The answer to the first option: for the two pieces in the memory window ($4EF5/$4EF6 + $C3), marks them (bit 6), clears their flip bits in their records ($BFC3 + 4 × piece, keeping the low two bits) and redraws them in the display ($9C8A), then shows ORIENTATION CORRECTED; with no piece, NOTHING IN MEMORY ($8009).

The answer to the second option: takes the puzzle number of the piece at the left of the memory window ($BFC0 + 4 × piece) and counts the pieces in memory with the same number; four or more shows A SOLUTION EXISTS, fewer NEED MORE PIECES; with nothing in memory, NOTHING IN MEMORY.
Shows the phone answer at offset X of str_phone_answers in the message line ($4376), waits 64 ticks and blanks the line again.
Writes the status line of the pocket computer, 62 characters from $3431 (SNOOZES:n LIFT INITS:n, then the password line PSW:) and their colours from $35C1, to $4376/$DB76.

Tests whether the piece being placed (shape in the sprite at $4D80/$4DC0) overlaps what slot Y already holds: builds a mask of the slot's border at $C100 and compares the AND of shape and slot with it, row by row. Carry clear: no overlap; carry set: overlap.

After a piece is placed: compares the 144 bytes of the display slot $8F with the nine solution images at $C9F0 (144 bytes apart). On a match with puzzle k: if already solved ($C8 + k) prints WE JUST DID THIS ONE ($82A2); otherwise marks it, counts it in $D8, copies that puzzle's password letter ($4FB5 + k) into the PSW line ($345D + k and the screen at $43A2 + k), removes its four pieces from memory ($817B for each), clears the display's work glyphs, redraws the memory window, beeps five times and clears the slot.

Removes from the memory list the piece whose number (low 6 bits) is A: shifts the rest of the list ($4EF5) and their colours ($4F25) down one, steps the memory window back if it now points past the end, and repaints the two memory slots.

Shows the 22-character message at (A low, X high) in the pocket computer's message line ($4376, yellow) with PUSH BUTTON beneath it ($439E, white), after the error tone; types it two characters a tick. Waits for fire to be pressed and released, then restores the status line ($8025).
The prompt under every message: "     " icon "PUSH BUTTON" icon, 22 characters in the $5800 alphabet ($F8/$F9 are the icons either side).

The pocket computer's messages, 22 characters each in the $5800 alphabet ($FA is the apostrophe): COLORS MUST MATCH ($821E), IMAGES CAN'T OVERLAP ($8234), NO IMAGE SELECTED ($824A), END OF MEMORY ($8260), CAN'T UNDO ($8276), TIME IS SUSPENDED ($828C), WE JUST DID THIS ONE ($82A2).
Address of display slot A's 144 bytes of glyph data in character set $5800: $5C50 + 144 × A, in $18/$19.

The random-number generator: a 16-bit shift register in $EB/$EC (feedback from bits 0 and 2 of $EB), and the result is $EB exclusive-ORed with the current raster line, so the timing of the call adds to the randomness.

The raster interrupt. In the shaft view ($1A = 0) there are two a frame. At line $AA, where the pocket computer begins: next interrupt at $FF, the panel's colours ($D021 = 0, $D022 = $0E, $D023 = 6) and character set $5800 ($D018 = $06). At line $FF: next interrupt at $AA, the shaft's colours ($D021 = $0C, $D022/$D023 from $21/$22) and character set $4800, and the count-down of $A4 that gates off voices 2 and 3. In a room ($1A set) there is one a frame, at line $FF, which re-arms itself and leaves the room's colours and character set alone; it runs the ball, the robots and the hit test from the interrupt ($9504, $8ECC, $92CB, saving zero page $79-$7D). Every frame: the tick $E0 and $3E, the game clock ($83A2) and the noise and protection check ($84FA). Measured: 120 entries in 120 frames in a room.

An interrupt handler that acknowledges the video chip and calls the routine whose address has been written into zero page $FC-$FE (`jsr $00FC`); installed briefly by the start-up and by $BEC2's callers.

Advances the game clock once a tick unless it is suspended ($D5) or already at six o'clock ($D4 = 6): $D1 counts 60 ticks, then the seconds $D2, minutes $D3 and hours $D4 (12-hour, 1-12) in decimal; $C1 counts the hours. At six o'clock $43 = $FF: time is up. The clock counts 60 ticks to the second, the NTSC frame rate. Live: 600 frames moved the clock on 10 seconds; the clock stood still with $D5 = 1.
Entry of game_clock that adds A minutes (decimal) to the clock; the caller sets decimal mode and masks interrupts. Used for the time a phone call costs (2 minutes) and other penalties.

Waits one tick and returns, unless time is up ($43 negative): then the end of the mission when time runs out. The screen shakes (random fine scroll) and flickers for 128 passes with the border white, goes blank, is cleared to a dark screen, the play area dissolves cell by cell into blanks, and the game goes to its end ($B786).
Fills the screen matrix $4000-$43FF with the blank glyph $53 (entered at $84D4 with another glyph in A).
Entry of clear_screen that fills the screen matrix with the glyph in A.
Fills colour RAM $D800-$DBFF with colour 9.

Called by the interrupt every frame: rotates the noise byte $E1; checks that $D024 (extra background colour 3) still holds $0A, the value the loader's last stage wrote at $B0AE, and if not jumps to $799A, the middle of an instruction where the byte $02 jams the processor: a protection check. Otherwise steps a second shift-register random source in $E3. Live: with $D024 set to 0 the processor jammed at $799A within 30 frames; the control run played on.
Draws the game clock on the pocket computer's status line: seconds, minutes and hours as two digits each ($8547) at $43AC + 6/3/0, with a blank instead of a leading zero in the hours.
Writes the decimal byte A as two digits of the $5800 alphabet ($80 + digit) at $43AC,y and $43AD,y.

Moves the lift down one step, unless the corridor below is in view ($1D): waits for raster line $A3, steps the shaft animation counters back, scrolls the shaft view down ($74C0), colours the corridors ($75A5), draws the new row ($7749), makes the lift's sound ($85B5) and waits until two ticks have passed.

Moves the lift up one step, unless the corridor above is in view ($1E): waits for raster line $3B, scrolls the shaft view up ($744B), draws the new row ($7631), sound ($85B5), steps the counters ($73CA), waits two ticks.

The lift's hum: raises the pitches $25 (by 4, up to $20) and $26 (by 3, up to $18), mixes them with the noise byte $E1 into the frequencies of voices 1 and 2, sustain $8F, sawtooth on voice 1 and noise on voice 2. The lift loop fades $25/$26 again when the lift stops.
Waits until the raster is past sprite 3's Y + $15, the bottom of sprite 3.

Moves the agent one step, called by the lift and room loops. With $43 set (dying, or time up) it runs the death sequence ($95E4). Waits until the raster is below sprite 3. If the agent is falling ($41 non-zero) it moves him down by $41/8 + 2 lines (at most 8), turns the fall into a landing when the feet meet solid ground (glyphs $47/$48, $8CC5) and, when the feet pass line $F8 (the agent has fallen out of the bottom of the room), keeps him falling until his top passes $F6 and sets $43 = 2: death by falling. Otherwise it waits for its turn ($3E against the speed $40), reads the stick ($87ED), steps the animation ($8817, $8859), keeps the agent out of the lift doors ($88F9), handles leaving the room ($8B6E), checks the robots and objects ($8E61, $9504), and sets the sprites for the new frame ($87D5, $8729).

Sets the agent's three sprites for animation frame $3F: pointers $43F9-$43FB from tbl_agent_pointers ($8D43), with sprite 2 switched off in the somersault frames $14-$19 and an extra pointer step for the walk frames 7-$0D. When the agent's facing ($50) differs from the way the frame is stored (byte 63 of the shape), mirrors the frame's three sprite shapes in place: every byte through the bit-reversal table $C500 and the three bytes of each row swapped, using the shape address from tbl_agent_shapes ($8D5F, written into the operands at $87AB-$87C4) and the length from $8D97. So each frame is stored once, facing one way.
Operand low byte of `ldx $6700,y` in agent_frame's mirroring loop: the frame's shape address, from tbl_agent_shapes.
High byte of the shape address read in agent_frame.
Operand low byte of `ldx $6702,y` in agent_frame: the shape address + 2.
High byte of the shape address + 2.
Operand low byte of `sta $6702,y` in agent_frame.
High byte for the `sta $6702,y`.
Operand low byte of `sta $6700,y` in agent_frame.
High byte for the `sta $6700,y`.
Operand low byte of `ldx $6701,y` in agent_frame.
High byte for the `ldx $6701,y`.
Operand low byte of `sta $6701,y` in agent_frame.
High byte for the `sta $6701,y`.
Copies the agent's positions ($2C-$31, X and Y of sprites 1-3) to the video chip and their ninth X bits ($32) into $D010 bits 1-3, with interrupts masked for the read-modify-write.

Reads left and right from the stick in port 2 while the agent is on his feet ($3F below $10): neither gives the standing frame $0E and no speed ($39 = 0); right gives facing $50 = $01 and speed +5, left $80 and -5.

Steps the animation frame $3F: on the ground, fire ($51, counted by the room loop) starts a somersault (frame $1B, with a sound on voice 3) and, while walking, the frame runs down from $0D to 0 and round again; while somersaulting it runs down to $10 and then lands on $0E, or $0D if the stick is still held.

Moves the agent's sprites by the current frame: when walking, $39 pixels sideways (with the ninth X bits in $32); in the somersault, by the per-frame offsets of tbl_somersault_dy1-3 ($8D07, $8D13, $8D1F) vertically and tbl_somersault_dx ($8D2B, $8D37) horizontally, negated when facing left, carrying into the ninth bits (the branch at $88B6 and $88DD/$88EB is patched between `bcc` and `bcs` for the sign).
The `bcc` at $88B6 in agent_move whose opcode is patched to $90 (bcc) or $B0 (bcs) by the sign of the vertical step, so that the carry of sprite 3's addition flips its ninth X bit correctly.
The branch at $88DD patched to `bcc` or `bcs` by the sign of the horizontal step (sprite 1's ninth bit).
The branch at $88EB patched the same way for sprite 2's ninth bit.

Keeps the agent from walking into a closed lift door: in the shaft view ($1A = 0) a door that is not open ($1F/$20 not $0B) pushes the agent back from it; in a room ($1A set) it computes the agent's box ($33-$38: top, bottom, left, right, middles) and resolves collisions with the room's walls and floors in four directions with $8AAA, $8ACD and $8CC5, sliding the agent back to the edge of the solid cell it moved into.
Tests for a solid cell to the right of the agent: at the middle height $37 and, except in the somersault frames $14-$18, eight lines higher as well. Carry set if solid.
The same test to the left of the agent ($3A).
A byte inside the code used as a scratch register by $8AF1: the three carries of the X subtraction, one per sprite.
Moves the agent's three sprites left by $E4 pixels, borrowing from the ninth X bits in $32 as needed (scratch in $8AF0).
Scratch byte for $8B23, as $8AF0 is for $8AF1.
Moves the agent's three sprites right by Y pixels, carrying into the ninth X bits in $32 (scratch in $8B22).
Moves the agent's three sprites up by $E4 lines.
Moves the agent's three sprites down by Y lines.

Checks whether the agent has walked out of the screen. To the right past X $164 or to the left before X $10 in a room: back into the corridor (the map marker $27 moves by 16, the shaft view is redrawn, the stack is reset and the lift loop restarts at $39CF). From the corridor, into the room on that side: the room number from the map ($FF96), its drawing ($A255, $A39C, $A2F7) and the room loop ($7249); a voice line ($BED9 with X = 1) on entering an ordinary room when an hour has passed ($C1).
The agent's top edge: Y of sprite 1 + the frame's offset from tbl_agent_top ($8DB3), at least $33.
The agent's feet: Y of sprite 1 + the frame's offset from tbl_agent_bottom ($8DCF).
The agent's left edge in X, from sprite 1's X and the frame's offsets ($8DEB facing left, $8E07 facing right); the ninth bit comes back in the carry.
The agent's right edge in X, the mirror of agent_left.

Tests the screen cell under a point: Y = raster line, X/carry = X position (nine bits). Converts to a cell of the screen at $4000 (row (Y - $32)/8, column (X - 24)/8) and returns carry set if the glyph there is a solid one, $45-$51 (floors, platforms and walls). Off the screen it returns carry clear. The row address is left in $7C/$7D.
Vertical step of sprite 1 in each of the twelve somersault frames ($10-$1B), signed: the arc of the jump.
Vertical step of sprite 2 in each somersault frame.
Vertical step of sprite 3 in each somersault frame.
Horizontal step of sprites 1 and 2 in each somersault frame, facing right (negated facing left).
Horizontal step of sprite 3 in each somersault frame.
Sprite pointer of the agent's first sprite for each of the 28 frames $00-$1B: walk $80-$98 (twice, for the two strides), standing $9C, $0F $9F, somersault $BD down to $A2.
Address of each frame's sprite shapes in bank 1 ($6000-$6FFF), for the in-place mirroring in agent_frame.
High bytes of tbl_agent_shapes, read with `ldy $8D60,x`.
Where the mirroring of each frame stops: $FC for the frames of three sprites, $BC and $7C for those of fewer.
Offset from sprite 1's Y to the agent's top edge, for each of the 28 frames.
Offset from sprite 1's Y to the agent's feet, for each frame.
Offset of the agent's left edge from sprite 1's X for each frame (used for the trailing edge when facing right and the leading edge when facing left).
Offset of the agent's other edge for each frame.
Moves the agent's three sprites one pixel right, in the video chip and in $2C-$31; when sprite 1's X wraps to 0, sets the ninth X bits of sprites 1-3 ($32 = $0E, $D010).
Moves the agent's three sprites one pixel left, clearing the ninth X bits when sprite 1's X is 0 before the step.
In the shaft view ($1A = 0) parks sprite 0 at X $A0 or $CA depending on which side of the lift the agent stands.
The agent's footsteps: in a room unless $4E is set (a robot is firing), on the walk frames 0, 7 and $10 a short pulse on voice 3 (pitch by facing), and the gate off on the frames $0E, $0A and 3.

Runs the robots, one pass for all of them every frame from the interrupt (with $1A set). While a robot's turn is delayed ($47 not $FF) it only counts. Otherwise, for each robot from the last ($54, steps of 6 bytes from $55), it interprets that robot's behaviour script: each robot has a script pointer ($55,x) into the script table at $2112, a current command with its count ($57,x), and flags ($56,x). Commands (top bits of the byte): relative jumps (add the low 6 bits to the pointer); tests that skip the next command or not: the agent to the left or right of the robot, the agent on its level (within 20 lines), a random bit; set the robot's mode; fire the zap ($8F3F); turn ($90B6, stepping its sprite pointer between $C0, facing one way, and $C6, the other); move ($90FB) for the command's count of frames. Then the zap and footstep sound bookkeeping. $FF ends a command and fetches the next.

A robot fires: the zap sound ($926F); every 32 frames the zap's count runs down and ends it below $94. Only on its own frame (the tick's low two bits equal to the robot's number) and only when the robot faces fully left or right (pointer $C0 or $C6): sprite 0 becomes the zap, placed 9 pixels right or 22 left of the robot (abandoned off the screen's right), its shape one of four random pointers $14-$17, X-expanded, flickering white and blue.

The script's test commands: compare the agent's X with the robot's (left or right, flipped by the robot's facing) and the agent's Y with the robot's (within $14 lines); the result decides whether the next command is skipped. A further form skips on a random bit ($904C).
Script command: sets the robot's mode bits (low two bits of $56,x) from the command, then fetches the next command. Mode 1 makes the robot move on alternate frames only (half speed, at $9111).

Script command: turns the robot towards the agent: compares the agent's and the robot's X and chooses the turn command that rotates the robot's pointer towards $C0 or $C6, unless it already faces that way.
Script command: wait; counts the command down every fourth frame ($9293).

Script command: turn one step every fourth frame, with the turning sound ($922A): the robot's sprite pointer ($43FC + robot) goes down towards $C0 or up towards $C6; the command ends when it gets there.

Script command: moves the robot one pixel (or a step on alternate frames in mode 1) left or right along its platform. Before each step it looks at the floor glyph below the robot's leading edge (through the robot's screen pointer $58/$59,x) and stops (sets bit 7 of $56,x and ends the command) where the floor ($45/$46) ends, so a robot never walks off its platform. When the agent is riding a lift platform (frame $0F) it checks the lift's glyphs too ($948C). Keeps the sub-cell position in $5A,x and carries into the ninth X bit.

End of one robot's turn: steps to the previous robot (6 bytes back) and loops; after the last, gates off the turning sound if no robot turned, the zap and footstep sounds as needed, and hides sprite 0 when the ball is not active ($6D).
Ends the current command and marks the robot blocked (bit 7 of $56,x).
Flashes the four robots' colours ($D02B-$D02E) between $4B and $4C every 8 ticks, unless $DC is set.
The robot-turning sound: voice 2 pulse with a pitch from the noise byte $E1, gated on; and the hum on voice 1 ($924E).
The robots' hum on voice 1: pulse wave at a pitch from the random byte $E3.
The zap's sound on voice 3: noise wave, pitch $0404, pulse from the tick, gate on.
Counts the robot's current command down (low 5 bits of $57,x); at zero ends it ($FF).
Up on the stick in a room: looks at the screen cell just above the agent's feet; anything other than the blank $53 is furniture or a terminal, and $97FB starts searching it (address in $10/$11).

Runs the floating ball (sprite 0) once a frame from the interrupt, when a ball is active ($6D positive) and the robots are not delayed ($47 = $FF). The ball follows a script of two-byte commands at $2232 + $6E (command, argument), with a counter $6F and a wait $70. Commands: 1 wait n frames ($70); 2 move by (high nibble, low nibble) as signed steps in X and Y; 3 home in on the agent's centre by up to n pixels in each direction; 4 jump to n; 5 jump by n if the counter is zero; 6 load the counter with n; 7 add n to the counter; others subtract n. Wait and move end the frame's commands; the others run on. After moving, ball_walls keeps the ball out of the walls.

Keeps the ball inside the room: wraps it from the bottom ($FB) to the top ($19), ignores it above line $33, and pushes it back out of any solid cell (glyphs below $4C, from $8CC5, or the lift platform, $948C) it has moved into, on its left, right, top and bottom edges, aligning it to the cell edge.

When the agent's frame is $0F, tests whether a screen cell (row pointer $7C/$7D + Y) lies on the lift platform the agent stands on, whose cells relative to $10/$11 (four rows of 8) are copied at $C100; carry set if that copy holds a solid glyph ($45-$51) there.
The agent's centre: middle of top and feet in $72 and middle of the left and right edges (X/2) in $73.

Has something touched the agent? Reads the sprite-sprite collision register $D01E. Not in the shaft view, not with $DC set, and not in the two special rooms $11 and $1B. Any of the agent's sprites (1-3) touching a robot (4-7) or, while the robots run, the zap (sprite 0) kills: $43 = 1, the robots stop ($47 = 0), the ball is switched off. When the ball is active, its touch is tested by distance as well: the ball's centre against the agent's centre must be within $40 (sum of X and Y distances, X doubled), and nearer than every robot, unless $85 is set; a near miss switches the ball off.

What happens when $43 is set. $FF (time up): the end of the game ($83FC). In the shaft view: nothing. In a room: the sound stops and the agent's three sprite shapes are copied into the work shapes at $4D80 ($972A). $43 = 2, a fall: the agent's sprites go off, voice line 7 (the scream) is played ($BED9). Otherwise, electrocuted: the agent flashes ($9765) and his shapes are eaten away bit by bit with random masks ($97E1) in 32 passes with the crackling sound. $43 = 3 also calls $AE23. Then the room is reset: the robots and the ball restart ($A102, the room record through $0E70, $A68B, $A714), the agent stands at the entrance ($ABE2, frame $0E, pointers back with $9718), ten minutes are added to the clock (`lda #$10 / jsr $83CC` in decimal mode), and play resumes. Live: setting $43 = 1 in a room ran the electrocution and moved the clock from 12:24:47 to 12:34:47.
The agent's three sprite pointers when standing: $9E, $9C, $9D.
The agent's three sprite colours: white (1) and light grey (11) twice.
Puts the agent's standing pointers and colours into sprites 1-3.
Copies the shapes of the agent's three current sprites into the work area at $4D80-$4E3F and points sprites 1-3 at the copies ($36-$38), so they can be dissolved without spoiling the originals.
One flash of the electrocution: a pause, the crackle ($97A4), the agent's sprites in white and grey, a pause, then the colours swapped.
The two colour pairs of death_flash: white/dark grey, grey/medium grey.
The second pair of death_flash colours.
A busy wait of about 13 × 256 loop passes (some 16,000 cycles), registers kept.
The electrocution crackle: voices 2 and 3 noise and pulse, random volume (0-7).
Returns in A a byte with one random bit clear (from tbl_bit_masks) and in X a random index 0-63, for eating away a sprite shape.
Eight masks with one bit clear: $FE, $FD, $FB, $F7, $EF, $DF, $BF, $7F.

Searching: the agent pushes up in front of something. Finds the object whose screen extent ($4F55-$4F58, start and end address) holds the cell in $10/$11 among the room's object records (6 bytes each from $4F55, ended by $FF; $86 counts in fours for the record's map flag). Saves the cells around the agent ($9BC8), takes the searching frame (frame + 1). The record's byte 4 ($4F59) is the search time left: 0 means already searched (straight to the result); $FF is a security terminal ($9D16). Otherwise shows the searching picture (built at $5000 from $9A5E) with a bar that fills while up is held, counting the time down by one a tick and stopping when the stick is released (the time left is kept, so a search can be resumed). When it reaches 0, the result ($98FB).

The contents of a searched object, byte 5 of its record ($4F5A): $FF nothing (the NOTHING HERE picture, $99E3); $FE a special object ($AA40); $FB a case handled by $A771; $FC a snooze password and $FD a lift-init password (picture from $9B31, the SNOOZES or LIFT INITS count in the status text incremented up to 9, $D7 counts passwords found); otherwise a puzzle piece: $D6 counts pieces found, its picture is built ($9C47), it is appended to the memory list ($4EF5) with the room's colour ($D021 into $4F25), and the first two pieces are also copied, inverted, into the display's two memory slots ($C690, $C840). The picture stays on screen until up is released or the agent dies; then the object is marked empty ($9B35).
Bit patterns for the search bar's last cell: $FF, $3F, $0F, $03 (four, three, two, one pixel pairs filled).

Three layouts of the searching box, 8 × 4 cells each (32 bytes, read by show_search_box from $99FE, $9A1E or $9A3E): glyph numbers, $52 for a blank cell and $00-$11 for the cells of the 144-byte picture built at $5000.
The second of the three searching-box layouts in tbl_search_layouts.
The third searching-box layout in tbl_search_layouts (the default operand of show_search_box).
The top of the picture shown while an object is searched, 64 bytes stored inverted; copied to $5000 at the start of a search, with $FF below it and the bar from $9A9E.
The first three bytes of the search bar, copied to $5078.
The picture shown when a search finds nothing (144 bytes, inverted, the size of a puzzle piece's picture), copied to $5000 by $99E3.
Low and high bytes of the two password pictures shown by a search: $3283 (snooze, $FC) and $31F3 (lift init, $FD).
High bytes of tbl_password_pics.

Marks object X as searched: contents $F0, the room's map flag cleared through ($87),$86, and its cells on screen blanked (4 rows of its width, keeping the floor glyphs $45-$4B on the lowest row) so the furniture disappears. A special object ($FE) is left alone.
Inverts the 144-byte picture at $5000 and shows it in the searching box.
Draws the searching box over the object: 8 × 4 cells from the layout table whose address is in A/X (written into the operand at $9BB1), in white, at $10/$11 and $14/$15.
Operand low byte of `lda $9A3E,x` in show_search_box: which of the three box layouts to draw.
High byte of the box layout's address.
Works out the screen address of the 8 × 4 cells above the agent ($10/$11, colour $14/$15) and saves them to $C100 (characters) and $C120 (colours) so the search box can be removed.
Puts back the 8 × 4 cells saved by save_search_area.

Builds the picture of puzzle piece A in $5000: from the piece's four-byte record at $BFC0, the solution image of its puzzle ($C9F0 + 144 × puzzle) ANDed with two mask shapes from the table at $2763, each mask inverted or not by the record's flag bits 0 and 1 (patched into the `lda #$00` operands at $9C64 and $9C6D). Then flips it by flag bits 3 (top to bottom, $7934) and 2 (left to right, $7999), so a piece can be found upside down or mirrored.
Immediate operand of `lda #$00` in build_piece: $00 or $FF, inverting the second mask for this piece (flag bit 1).
Immediate operand of `lda #$00` in build_piece: $00 or $FF, inverting the first mask (flag bit 0).
Entry of build_piece's end: points $18/$19 and the flip routines' operands at the glyphs at $5000 + A, then applies the flips in $E4; used by phone_answer_orient to show a piece the right way round.
Sets the pointers for build_piece: $E6/$E7 = the piece's record ($BFC0 + 4A), $E8/$E9 = its puzzle's solution image, and $C4-$C7 the two mask shapes ($2763 + 144 × mask number).

The security terminal. Blanks the screen, saves the screen ($4000-$43FF to $C100-$C4FF) and colour RAM ($D800-$DBFF to $0400-$07FF), and the video chip's sprite and colour registers on the stack. Draws the terminal's screen from two run-length lists of (count, value) pairs: characters from $3633 and colours from $37A9 (value $FF = the room's colour), 25 rows; sets the colours from tbl_terminal_colours, eight sprites from tbl_terminal_sprites and their pointers ($18-$1D), and the character set two below. Runs the terminal ($9F0E), then restores everything. Live: started from the room loop in room $1C, it showed SECURITY TERMINAL 28.
Operand high byte of `lda $3634,x` in security_terminal: the run-length list's page, stepped when X wraps.
Operand high byte of `lda $3633,x` in security_terminal, stepped with $9E0B.
Colours for $D021-$D02E while the terminal is shown: background 9, extra colours $0B/$0C (or the room's), and the eight sprite colours (patched with the room's colour at $9EED-$9EF0).
Entries of tbl_terminal_colours patched with the room's colour: $D022 here, $D023 after it, and the four sprite colours at $9EED-$9EF0.
tbl_terminal_colours +2: the terminal's second multicolour, $0C, or $0B when the room's colour is grey ($0C).
The four sprite colours in tbl_terminal_colours that terminal set-up patches with the room's colour.
X and Y of the eight sprites of the terminal screen and their ninth X bits: the screen's decorations and the pointer.
Sprite pointers of the terminal's eight sprites, $18-$1D.

The security terminal's menu: writes the room number $7E in decimal as two digits into the title line (the 00 of SECURITY TERMINAL 00, at $A048/$A049; room $1C shows as 28, seen live), then types the screen line by line, one line a frame (24-character lines from str_terminal at the offsets in tbl_terminal_lines), with a row of three $95 glyphs (`***`) at the top. Puts the pointer `==>` at LOG OFF ($8A = 2) and loops: fire (on a fresh press, $DE) carries out the choice ($A0DE); up and down move the pointer between the three choices (rows apart by tbl_terminal_steps) with a short delay ($9791).
Rows between the terminal's choices, for moving the pointer: 2 and 6 (the second choice is two rows lower than the first, the last six lower than the second).
Draws the terminal's pointer, the three glyphs `==` and `>` from $9FFA, at $10/$11.
The pointer's three glyphs: = = > in the $4800 alphabet ($96, $96, $97).
Offsets into str_terminal of the terminal screen's fifteen text rows, read last first ($00 = the blank line, $18 the title, $30, $48 ... $90 the choices and $A8 LOG OFF.).
Copies one 24-character line of str_terminal, from offset X, to the screen at $10/$11.

The security terminal's text, 24-character lines in the $4800 alphabet: a blank line, SECURITY TERMINAL 00 *** (the room number is written over the 00), SELECT FUNCTION, RESET LIFTING PLATFORMS / IN THIS ROOM., TEMPORARILY DISABLE / ROBOTS IN THIS ROOM., LOG OFF.
The two digits of the room number in SECURITY TERMINAL 00, written by terminal_menu ($A048 tens, $A049 units).
The units digit of the terminal's room number, and the rest of str_terminal after it (the choices and LOG OFF.).

Carries out the terminal choice under the pointer ($8A). The two password functions first check the password ($A1A1); without one nothing happens. $8A = 0, reset lifting platforms ($A102). $8A = 1, disable robots: $47 = $40, which stops the robots and the ball until the robots' counter, stepped every fourth tick, climbs back to $FF (764 ticks); if no ball is active, bit 0 of the saved sprite enable on the stack is cleared so the ball stays off. $8A = 2, LOG OFF: drops the return addresses and leaves the terminal. Live (the snooze's effect): $47 = $40 kept the robots still for 300 frames and returned to $FF after about 764 ticks.

Resets the lifting platforms of the room: for each platform in the room's list at ($81) (a position, a height, a list of $FF-ended bytes), blanks its cells ($AC22 gives the address, three cells wide); then finds the room in tbl_room_platform_ptrs ($1FDA) and copies its original platform list back from the address in $2016, and draws every platform again ($AC55). In a room the death sequence redraws ($43 set), the screen addresses are shifted down by $81 pages to draw into the copy at $C100.

For the two password functions ($8A = 0 lift init, 1 snooze): blanks the three rows under the choice, then looks at the matching count in the status text ($3439 + 0 for SNOOZES, + $0D for LIFT INITS, digits in the $5800 alphabet). Above 0: decrements it and shows PASSWORD ACCEPTED; otherwise PASSWORD REQUIRED (carry from the comparison). Then a long delay and the choice's text drawn back.
Screen addresses ($A223/$A224 low, $A225/$A226 high) of the rows of the two password choices: $4122 and $419A.
High bytes of tbl_terminal_choice_addr.
Offsets of the two counters' digits in the status text at $3439: $0D (LIFT INITS) and $00 (SNOOZES).
PASSWORD REQUIRED and PASSWORD ACCEPTED, 19 characters each in the $4800 alphabet, shown by check_password.
Offsets into str_terminal of the lines to redraw under each choice after a password check.

The wipe between a room and the corridor: silences the sound, hides the sprites and, two ticks a step, blanks two rows of the screen moving outwards from the middle ($41E0) while two raster bands ($8B going up, $8C going down) paint the background colour black between them, until the bottom band reaches line $FB. In the shaft view the lower band stops at the pocket computer ($AA).
Fills one 40-cell row at $10/$11 and one at $12/$13 with the blank glyph.

Reveals a room drawn in the buffer at $C100-$C4FF: from the middle of the screen outwards, one pair of rows every second tick, copies the buffer's rows (screen $C100-, colours $C400 area to $D800-) to the screen, while two raster bands ($8B moving down from line $32, $8C up from $FC) paint the background black outside the revealed part and the room's colour ($8D) inside. When the bands meet, the agent stands (frame $0E) and the room's sprites are switched on ($8E).
Copies one 40-cell row from ($12) to ($10) and one from ($16) to ($14): a step of room_wipe_in.

Draws room $7E into the buffer at $C100-$C4FF (screen) and $C400 area (colours) before it is shown. Stops the robots ($47 = 0), clears the sprite Y positions, fills the buffer with blanks and selects character set $4800. Reads the room's record through the pointer table at $0E70: background colour ($8D), the two multicolours ($D022, $D023), the floor colour ($E6); then the floors, as (address, length) triples ending with $FF, drawn with the floor glyph $45 and end glyph $46; the side walls ($47 left, $48 right, 25 rows); the gaps, as (address, glyph) pairs, five blanked cells above a glyph; the agent's start ($ABE2), the robots ($A68B) and the ball ($A714); the sprite multicolours, the robots' two colours ($4B/$4C), the sprites to switch on ($8E); then the lifting platforms (list at ($81), each drawn by $AC55) and the furniture: for each object an index into tbl_furniture ($232C, five bytes: shape address, width and height, search time) and its contents; draws its shape (blank where the contents are $F0, already searched) and fills its search record at $4F55 (screen extent, search time, contents). Rooms $11 and $1B, the code rooms, get their big screen ($A5C9).

Extra drawing for the two code rooms ($7E = $11 or $1B): a large framed screen of 13 rows by 32 columns in the buffer (borders of glyphs 3 and 4, a top and bottom row of glyphs 1 and $10/$06, colour $0E and $0C), the 144-byte picture at $3063 copied to $5000, and sprites 4-7 set up from tbl_code_room_sprites: pointers $10 (the hand), $33, $34, $35, their colours and positions, sprite 7 multicolour, sprite 0 pointer $1E.
Sprite pointers of the code room's sprites 4-7: $10 (the hand), $33, $34, $35.
X and Y of the code room's sprites 4-7: ($3C,$53), ($A0,$E2), ($B8,$E2), ($AC,$E2).
Colours of the code room's sprites 4-7: cyan (3), black, black, white.

Sets up the room's robots from its record at ($18),y: all four robots (sprites 4-7) facing one way (pointer $C0), multicolour, unexpanded. For each robot until $FF: its script's start in the script table ($55,x), mode 1 ($56,x), no command ($57,x = $FF), Y = row × 8 + $1F, X = (column + 2) × 8 with the ninth bit, its screen address under it ($58/$59,x via $AC22) and sub-cell position 3 ($5A,x). $54 ends as the last robot's offset (6 bytes a robot), or $FF for none.
Sets up the room's ball from its record: none if the byte is $FF ($6D = $FF); otherwise the ball's script start ($6E), its X and Y, pointer $1F, black, and $6D = 0 (active).
Animates the code room's big screen every sixteen ticks: random sprite multicolours and random light colours (8-15, $A921) in four cells of the colour RAM at $DB81-$DB86.

The musical puzzle of the code rooms, entered when the agent searches the room's computer (contents $FB). The sixteen tones (eight notes in two octaves) are shuffled in tbl_tones ($B229); $74 of them (the room's level: $75 for room $11, $76 for room $1B) are hidden at random among the 32 squares of the screen (tbl_square_tones at $A8BE, $FF for empty), each square drawn ($A8DE) and played once ($A950). The hand (sprite 4) then moves over the 8 × 4 squares; fire on a square plays its tone. The player must press the hidden tones in rising order: a tone lower than the last one ($78) starts the count ($77) again. When all $74 have been pressed in order, a password is earned (LIFT INITS for an even level, SNOOZES for an odd one, up to 9; both levels start at 2), the screen flashes ($AA10), and the room's level rises by one (to at most 14) for the next time. Fire below the squares leaves.
The code room's 32 squares (8 columns by 4 rows): the tone hidden under each, or $FF for none; filled at random by code_room_puzzle.
Colours code-room square X (column X AND 7, row X/8) in the colour RAM from $D8A4: 4 × 3 cells of colour $0D.
A random colour from 8 to 15.
Sets the SID for the code room's tones: attack/decay $5A, sustain/release $58 on voice 3, pulse widths 0, volume 5.

Shows and plays tone A of square X: sprite 0 moves to the square, coloured by the note (tbl_tone_colours); the note (A AND 7) from tbl_tone_lo/hi, one octave lower when bit 3 is clear, goes to the three voices an octave apart; pulse waves gated on for 32 ticks with a pulse width that moves with the tick, the hand still movable ($3DC2); then sprite 0 off and the gates closed.
Low bytes of the eight notes of the code room's tones (with tbl_tone_hi: $430F, $4B45, $547D, $5983, $6479, $70C7, $7E97, $861E, a rising scale).
High bytes of the code room's eight notes.
Colour of each of the eight notes, shown on sprite 0 over the square: red, orange, yellow, light green, light blue, blue, purple, red.
Paints the code room's 8 × 4 squares in colour A in a chequer pattern (alternating 0 and 1 by cell), the reward flash when called repeatedly with A alternating.

The object with contents $FE, Elvin's control: with any letter of the password line ($345D-$3465) still blank, nothing happens. With all nine found, the mission is won: $DC = 1, a frame shape in sprite 7 (pointer $36) opens over the screen, a 6 × 5 block of characters and colours from $2611/$25F3 is drawn at $4301, and the frame closes again row by row. Then the end picture: video bank 3 (screen $C000, character set $D000-$D7FF in the RAM under the I/O area), the screen copied from $DC00-$DFFF to $C000-$C3FF with all RAM banked in, the colours from $F800-$FBFF to colour RAM; voice line 4 ($BED9); the mouth animation, alternating the two mouth pictures ($AB84, $AB75) for the durations in tbl_end_timing while random cells twinkle ($ABBA); and finally $BECD and the score ($B786). Live: forced by filling the password line and starting here; Elvin's face appeared, talking, then the tally.
Operand low byte of `ldx $AB67,y` in elvin_terminal's mouth animation: $67 points at the NTSC timings, and detect_pal writes $6E on PAL to use the PAL timings instead.
The second `ldx` of the mouth animation's timings, patched like $AB2B.
The third `ldx` of the mouth animation's timings, patched like $AB2B.

How long each step of the end picture's mouth animation lasts on an NTSC machine (60 frames a second), in calls of end_twinkle: $40, $28, $28, $20, $2C, $20, $10. Read when detect_pal leaves the operands at $67.

The same seven durations for PAL (50 frames a second), five sixths of the NTSC values: $35, $21, $21, $1B, $25, $1B, $0D, so that the mouth keeps time with the speech, which runs from a CPU timer at the same speed on both.
Draws the closed mouth into the end picture: 13 glyphs from tbl_mouth_closed at the screen positions $C2B6 + tbl_mouth_cells.
Draws the open mouth: 13 glyphs from tbl_mouth_open at the same positions.
The 13 glyphs of the open mouth in the end picture.
The 13 glyphs of the closed mouth.
Offsets from $C2B6 of the mouth's 13 cells, over four rows of the picture ($00-$02, $28-$2A, $50-$53, $79-$7B).

X times: for six random cells of the end picture's colour RAM (a random low byte, avoiding a band of values, written into the `sta $D800` at $ABD8) sets a random light colour (8-15 from the noise byte via $84FA), a tick apart. The twinkling lights of the end picture.
Operand low byte of `sta $D800` in end_twinkle: a random cell of the end picture's colour RAM.

Places the agent at the room's entrance from the room record at ($18),y: the left or right entry ($7F) gives X for sprites 1-3, the Y of sprite 2, with sprites 1 and 3 at +12 and +21, and the ninth X bits.

Address in the room buffer of the cell at row ($81),y and column ($81),y+1 of a room list: row × 40 + column + $C100 in $10/$11, and the matching colour address ($D800 + ...) in $14/$15. Y is advanced past the row.
Draws a lifting platform's top, three glyphs $49-$4B from $0DB4, in colour $84, at $10/$14.
Draws the lifting platform's two-row cap, glyphs $4F-$51 ($0DBA) and below them $4C-$4E ($0DB7), in colour $84.

The lifting platforms: when the agent stands still (frame $0E), finds the platform under his feet in the room's platform list at ($81) (each entry: row, column, height, a movement count, a list) by his feet's row ($52) and column ($53). Up on the stick raises it ($ACF6) and down lowers it ($AD81), once per press ($83); otherwise it clears $83 and $85. A death meanwhile ($43) goes to agent_death.

Raises the platform under the agent one cell at a time, the agent's sprites moving up with it 4 lines a step ($AECC): redraws the cap and the column below as it rises and updates the list's height and count. If the agent is killed while it moves, $43 = 3 (the death redraws the platform).
Lowers the platform under the agent, the mirror of platform_up, moving the agent down 4 lines a step ($AEDF), unless its count is already 0; $85 is set while it moves (no ball collision then).
Blanks a platform's column, three cells wide, $E5 + 1 rows upwards from $10.

In a room, with the agent not already falling: on the walking and standing frames (0, 7, 6, $0D, $0E, $10), tests the cells under the front and back of his feet ($AEB7, offsets by frame and facing); with nothing solid under either, and not at the screen's edge, starts a fall ($41 + 1). Solid ground clears $41 and $42.
Entry of check_ground that skips the room and falling tests: used by agent_update after moving.
Tests the cell under one foot: X or Y (by the facing $50) added to the agent's left edge $E6/$E7, at the line $E8 below his feet ($8CC5). Carry set if solid.
Moves the agent's three sprites up 4 lines (registers and $2D-$31).
Moves the agent's three sprites down 4 lines.
Moves the cell pointers $10/$11 and $14/$15 up six rows (subtracts $F0).
Moves the cell pointers back by $118 (a page and $18).
Moves the cell pointers up five rows (subtracts $C8).
Moves the cell pointers up four rows (subtracts $A0).
Moves the cell pointers up one row (subtracts $28).
Moves the cell pointers down six rows (adds $F0).
Moves the cell pointers down one row (adds $28).
Moves the cell pointers down two rows (adds $50).

Sets up the shaft view when the agent comes out of a room: the agent's sprites in the lift, the room's sprites to show ($8E = $CF), the background colour $8D = $0C, the shaft's two colours ($21/$22) chosen by the map column ($27) from tbl_shaft_colours, screen off, character set $4800, both corridor doors closed ($1F = $20 = $FF), the map marker two lines up; draws the shaft and pocket computer ($72A2), a corridor ($7850), clears the message window, draws the map ($B699), moves the screen to the buffer and blanks it for the wipe, sets the lift car's sprites ($B750, $AFEF), and turns the screen on.
The lift car: sprite 7 (pointer $11, white) and sprite 0 (pointer $12, Y-expanded multicolour) in the shaft's colours ($21/$22).
The first colour of the lift shaft for each of the eight shafts (by map column): $02, $04, $0C, $0D, $05, $06, $08, $0E.
The second colour of the lift shaft for each shaft: $0A, $07, $0F, $01, $0D, $03, $09, $07.

For a new game, puts back every room's lifting platforms: a list of (address, ...) pairs at $1FDA, each the start of a room's platform list in its record, receives the original bytes from the copy at $1F64 onwards (a running index, the source page self-modified at $B079), each list up to its $FF, stepping the list pointer by two between rooms ($BEB8).
Copies bytes from the platform originals ($1F64 + X, page in the operand at $B079) to ($E4),y up to and including an $FF.
Operand high byte of `lda $1F64,x` in copy_to_ff: the page of the platform originals, stepped when X wraps.

Gives every robot in the stronghold a random behaviour for this game: for each of the 30 room records (pointers at $20D6), finds the robot list after the floor list and, for each robot (3 bytes), writes a random script number from tbl_robot_scripts ($2212): one of the first 16 entries, or of the second 16 when the room also has a ball.
Chooses this game's password: one of the eight nine-letter words at $208E at random, copied to $4FB5-$4FBD; the password line of the pocket computer ($345D-$3465) is blanked.

Makes the nine puzzle images at $C9F0: 162 eight-byte blocks, each one of sixteen patterns from tbl_puzzle_patterns ($26E3) chosen at random, the pointer stepped by 8 each time ($BEB8); then gives each of the nine images its frame ($B137).

Draws a frame round the 144-byte image at ($18): the top row of each column set solid ($FF every 8 bytes from $28 down), the left and right edges set (ORed with $C0 and $03), and the image's corner bytes cleared.

Cuts the nine puzzles into four pieces each (36 records of 4 bytes at $BFC0-$C04F): clears a 16 × 16 table of used mask pairs at $C100, shuffles the sixteen mask numbers in tbl_tones ($B229: 64 swaps of entry 2 with a random entry 3-15), then for each puzzle gives its four pieces the puzzle number, the same first mask (the shuffled entry for that puzzle), the piece number 0-3 in the low bits of the flags with random flip bits ($0C), and two second masks chosen at random so that no pair of masks is used twice ($B239): pieces 3 and 2 share one, pieces 1 and 0 the other. build_piece uses the low two bits to invert the masks, so the four pieces are the image cut by a mask and its complement in each direction, and they overlap.

Sixteen numbers shuffled at run time by two users: make_pieces fills it with 0-15 and shuffles it for the order of the mask shapes at the start of a game; code_room_puzzle fills it with 0-7 and 9-16 (the second octave's notes carry bit 3) and shuffles it for its tones.
Entry 2 of tbl_tones, the one make_pieces swaps with random entries while shuffling.
The second half of tbl_tones: 8-15 for make_pieces, 9-16 for code_room_puzzle.

Tests whether mask $E7 can pair with the piece's first mask ($BFC1,x): not the same, and neither ordering of the pair marked in the table at $C100. If free, marks both orderings ($FF) and returns carry clear; otherwise carry set.

Hides this game's items in the furniture: every content byte in the list of furniture slots (pointers at $30F3) is set to $FF (nothing); then the 36 puzzle pieces (0-$23) each go into a random empty slot ($B2A4), and nine snooze passwords ($FC) and nine lift-init passwords ($FD) likewise.
Picks a random furniture slot from the list at $30F3 (an even index) until it finds one still holding $FF; returns its address in $18/$19.

Generates this game's stronghold map. The 32 room numbers at $FFCC-$FFEB (0-$1F) are shuffled within four groups of eight. The map's glyph data $FC00-$FF2F is filled with $FF (solid), the room grid $FF96-$FFCB (9 columns by 6 rows) with $FF (empty) and the map's cell table $FF30-$FF95 with $FC. Then rooms are placed on the grid ($B3FC with the room grid placement $B450) in columns 1-7 of random rows, and joined: rooms of the first group into the left columns with corridors ($B488, direction flags in $E8: $40 left, $80 right, $C0 both), the second group spread over random columns, the third and fourth paired along each column. Finally the map marker starts at ($6B, $B8), the top of the first shaft.
A random row of the map grid, 0-5.

Puts room A at column X, row Y of the map: claims the first free grid square at or after it ($B450), then cuts the room's shape out of the map's glyph data ($18/$19 from $B516): rooms below $10 one of four 24-byte shapes from tbl_room_shapes chosen by bits 0 and 3 of the room number, the others ($10-$1F) 16-byte shapes from further on in the table, ANDed into the map; rooms $18 and above go one cell further on ($BEB8).

Finds a free square of the room grid ($FF96 + 9 × row + column) starting from column X, row Y, moving down a row at a time (wrapping) and then to the next column (wrapping at 8 to 1), and stores room A there.

Draws the corridors that join the room at column X, row Y to its neighbours in the direction(s) given by $E8 ($40 one side, $80 the other, $C0 both): looks along the row (and up and down the column by nine squares) for the next occupied square that may be joined ($B500), and cuts corridor and shaft segments into the map's glyph data between them ($B516, $B538).

Whether a room number in A may be joined in the current direction: rooms $10-$17 are not joined from one side ($E8 bit 7 clear), and rooms $18 and above not at all from the other. Carry set: not joinable.
Address in the map's glyph data of grid square (X, Y), in $18/$19: $FB78 + $88 × (row + 1) + 16 × column - 8, built by repeated additions with add_to_ptr ($BEB8).

Cuts a corridor into the map glyphs at $18/$19: a vertical shaft piece (8 bytes from tbl_shaft_mask $B63D) when $E8 bit 6 is set, and a horizontal corridor piece (bytes 16-23 of tbl_corridor_mask $B62D, one cell back when X is 0) when bit 7 is set.
Six glyphs (48 bytes) copied into the display's glyphs at $5F80-$5FAF when the map is shown, replacing the last glyphs of the piece display; what they draw on the map was not checked.
Masks ANDed into the map's glyph data to cut out the rooms: 24-byte and 16-byte shapes, $E7 for the walls and $00 where the room is open.
Mask bytes for a horizontal corridor on the map (bytes 16-23 used).
Mask bytes for a vertical lift shaft segment on the map.

Switches the pocket computer's display to the map: waits a tick, clears the message window, saves the display's glyphs ($5C50-$5FAF) to $C690-$C9EF and copies the map's glyph data ($FC00-$FF2F) into their place, and the marker glyphs from $B56D; then draws the map's frame ($B699).

Draws the map in the display: a frame of glyphs $F0-$F5 in yellow, the 18 × 6 cells of the map from the cell table $FF30 in green, and the map marker in sprite 6 (a small square, shape at $4D80) at ($27, $28).
Entry of draw_map_frame's end: sets sprite 6's pointer to $36.
Reveals on the map the room on the side the agent left the corridor by ($7F against $80 chooses the half-cell), then falls into reveal_map_cell.

Reveals the map cell under the marker: index = ($27 - $68)/8 + 18 × (($28 - $B8)/8) + $E6, and the cell table entry at $FF30 + index becomes glyph $8A + index, the cell's own glyph in the display. Cells start as $FC (blank), so the map fills in as the agent explores. Returns the glyph.

The end of a game, won, lost or out of time: silences the SID, hides the sprites, clears the screen and colour RAM, selects character set $4800 and turns the screen on. Draws a box ($B996, $B9CF, $B9E1) and inside it the tally's labels (pointers at tbl_tally_labels, lengths at $B988, row steps at $B98F), the fifth line MISSION COMPLETE, or MISSION TERMINATED at $B957 when time ran out ($D4 = 6). Voice line 0 unless time ran out; then the normal interrupt again ($BEC2), the score ($BA08), the high score and name entry ($BC04), the prompt from $BDBD, and waits for RESTORE or RUN/STOP ($BE2D returning $F0) before restarting at $388C.

The end screen's text in the $4800 alphabet: PUZZLE PIECES FOUND ($B8A7), PASSWORDS FOUND ($B8BA), PUZZLES SOLVED ($B8C9), SECONDS REMAINING ($B8D7), MISSION COMPLETE ($B8E8), T O T A L   S C O R E ($B8F8), THIS SURPASSES THE PREVIOUS HIGH SCORE OF ($B90F), HALL OF FAME ($B94A) and M I S S I O N   T E R M I N A T E D ($B957).
Part of str_tally: THIS SURPASSES THE PREVIOUS (from $B90D) and HIGH SCORE OF (from $B92A) are copied as two 29-character lines by hall_of_fame.
The second line of the high-score message within str_tally, HIGH SCORE OF, then HALL OF FAME and MISSION TERMINATED.
Addresses of the seven tally labels in str_tally, drawn by end_of_game from the last up.
High bytes of the addresses in tbl_tally_labels.
Length - 1 of each tally label.
Rows to move up between the tally's labels.
Draws a row of the end screen's box: 37 cells of glyph $CA, then ten edge glyphs from $B9AD at the offsets in $B9B7.
Glyphs and their column offsets for the box rows: corners and edges ($C8, $C9, $CB, $CC) and the colour-RAM edge marks, offsets $00, $01, $26, $27 ...
Column offsets of the box glyphs in tbl_box_glyphs.
Column offsets of the box's lower edge glyphs.
Draws the box's left and right edges on one row: four glyphs from $B9DD at the offsets in $B9B7.
The four side glyphs of the box: $CD, $D8, $D7, $D0.
Draws the box's bottom row: glyph $D3 from column $2A to $4D and fourteen edge glyphs from $B9FA.
The box's bottom edge glyphs, $CD-$D6.

Works out and shows the score (decimal, $D9 units, $DA hundreds, $DB ten-thousands): puzzle pieces found ($D6) and passwords found ($D7) at 100 points each, puzzles solved ($D8) at 500 each, each line shown as count × points = total ($BB7C template). If the mission was completed with time left, the seconds remaining until six o'clock (from the clock $D2/$D3/$D4, 12 o'clock counted as 0) at one point each, and a bonus of 1,000 for the mission; when time ran out, 000. Then the total ($BB08). Live: a forced win at 12:24:47 with nothing found scored 20,113 seconds + 1,000 = 21,113.
The digits of the mission bonus shown on the end screen: 1, 0, 0, 0.
compute_score's path when time ran out: moves the pointer down six rows ($AF26), then shows the total.
Prints the six-digit decimal number in $E4-$E6 at $10,y onwards, without leading zeros (a single 0 for zero).
Entry of print_bcd6 with the column in Y already set.
Writes digit A (as glyph $8B + A of the $4800 alphabet) at ($10),y in white.
Entry of print_digit that writes the glyph in A (not a digit) at ($10),y in white.
Adds A (decimal) to the score's units $D9, carrying into $DA and $DB; entered at $BB55 to add to the hundreds.
Entry of add_score that adds A to the hundreds $DA.
Adds A (decimal) to the three-byte number $E4-$E6; entered at $BB6D for the middle byte.
Entry of add_e4 that adds A to the middle byte $E5.
Draws the template of one tally line, 13 cells from $BB8C in the colours from $BB99: the count, `×` and `00`, `=` and `00`.
The tally line's glyphs: blanks, the multiplication sign $D9, zeros ($8B) and the equals sign ($96).
Colours of the tally line's cells: white and yellow.
Counts Y into $E4 and adds 100 points per unit to the score (decimal): for pieces and passwords.
Counts Y × 5 into $E4 and adds 500 points per unit: for puzzles solved.
Prints the decimal count $E4 in the tally line twice: as the count (columns 0-1) and in the product (columns 9-10), with the glyph $8C after the count.

The high-score table, kept at $CF00-$CF77 while the machine stays on: 15 entries of 8 bytes, a three-byte decimal score and a five-character name. Finds the score's place ($BE1D compares with each entry from the bottom), moves the lower entries down one and writes the new score in. If it beats the top entry, shows THIS SURPASSES THE PREVIOUS HIGH SCORE OF and the old top score. Then lists all fifteen entries in three columns of five (score and name, in purple), and if the score made the table, asks for the player's name: ENTER YOUR I.D. CODE ON THE KEYBOARD, five characters typed with the keyboard ($BE2D), DEL to rub out, RETURN to finish; stored into the entry.
Screen offsets (from $4300) of the name field of each of the fifteen hall-of-fame places.
ENTER YOUR I.D. CODE ON THE KEYBOARD, 36 characters in the $4800 alphabet.
HIT RESTORE OR RUN/STOP FOR NEW GAME, 36 characters in the $4800 alphabet ($DD for the slash).
Colours of the 36 characters of str_new_game: green (5) and yellow (7) by word.
24 bytes that read in PETSCII as fragments like "HI2 0:HI" and "HI=HI2I"; no reference to them was found (searched with opcodes.py --refs); possibly assembler leftovers.
Compares the three-byte decimal score $D9-$DB with the hall-of-fame entry at ($18): carry set if the entry is higher or equal.

Scans the keyboard matrix itself (CIA 1 port A as output): returns $FF with no key, or the code of the key found from tbl_keys (a letter or digit in the $4800 alphabet, 0 RETURN, 1 DEL, $F0 RUN/STOP, $FD/$FE others), once per press ($DF holds it until the keys are released).
The 64 keys of the matrix, row by row, as codes for read_key: letters and digits in the $4800 alphabet, 0 for RETURN, 1 for DEL, $F0 for RUN/STOP, $FF for keys the name entry ignores.
Adds A to the pointer $18/$19.
Installs the game's interrupt handlers: IRQ $82F4 and, entering at $BECD, NMI $388C (the restart, reached by RESTORE).
Points the NMI vector at $388C, the game's restart: RESTORE starts a new game.
The number of the voice line being spoken, kept by say_line.

Speaks voice line X through the speech driver: silences the SID, swaps the IRQ for the minimal $8396 (which only counts the tick with the `inc $E0 / rts` kept in zero page $FC-$FE) so that the speech NMIs run undisturbed, and starts the line ($0880). Lines 4 and 5 return at once and play on while the game continues; the others wait until the driver reports the end ($FF query). After lines other than 0, 2, 3 and 7 the normal interrupt comes back ($BEC2) at the next frame top. Callers: lines 2 and 3 at the start ($39B0, $39BB), 1 on entering a room when an hour has passed ($8BCC), 7 the fall ($9611), 5 the time-up sequence ($8413), 4 the end picture ($AB25), 0 the end screen ($B87D).

The end picture's character set, glyphs $00-$7F (RAM under the I/O area, shown through video bank 3 at $D000): multicolour glyphs of Professor Elvin Atombender's face and his control room. Moved here from $C800 by move_high_tables at the start; the CPU never reads it after that, only the video chip.
In the start-up's copy at $396B (port $21, character ROM) the ROM's letters A-Z start here and are copied into both game character sets; the RAM beneath is part of the end picture's character set.

In the start-up's copy at $3980 the processor port is $21, so the CPU reads the character ROM here: $D180-$D1CF are the ROM's digits 0-9, copied into both game character sets. The RAM beneath holds glyphs $30-$7F of the end picture's character set (the rest of gfx_end_charset_1).
The end picture's character set, glyphs $80-$FF.

The end picture's screen: 1000 characters (25 rows of 40) and 24 unused bytes, under CIA 1 and CIA 2. Moved here from $C400 at the start and copied to the bank-3 screen at $C000 by elvin_terminal; the mouth cells at $C2B6 are then animated.

The speech data's phrase table, at the sample base the game gives the driver ($E000): eight entries of four bytes for voice lines 0-7, each two offsets from $E000: the line's pitch commands and its frame headers (speech_lookup). Line 6 is never asked for by the game.

The voice lines' pitch commands, read by speech_pitch_step: for each line a list of entries giving a period length and a count with an index into the pitch step table. Line 0's list starts here, lines 1-7 at $E0A8, $E0D2, $E0F2, $E134, $E154, $E188 and $E18A.

The voice lines' frame headers, four bytes each, read by speech_frame_header: the encoding of the frame's samples (1-bit, 2-bit or 4-bit), repeat counts and flags, and the offset of the frame's sample data from $E000. Line 0's headers start here, the others at $E31A, $E35E, $E392, $E3C6, $E3E6, $E46E and $E476.

Compressed speech samples, first part ($E52D-$E92C): packed 1, 2 or 4 bits a sample as each frame header says, decoded into the speech buffer at $0800 by the frame decoders. The recordings were made by Electronic Speech Systems according to the published credits.
Compressed speech samples, second part ($E92D-$ED2C).
Compressed speech samples, third part ($ED2D-$F12C).
Compressed speech samples, fourth part ($F12D-$F52C).
Compressed speech samples, last part ($F52D-$F771), up to the end of the file words.
The last bytes the file words loads, $FF padding after the samples.
The end picture's colour RAM, 1000 nibbles (bit 3 set for multicolour cells) and 24 unused bytes. Moved here from $C000 at the start and copied to $D800 by elvin_terminal.
